questions.title: Nucleotide to nucleoside conversion
questions.question: A nucleotide is converted into a nucleoside by the removal of a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Removing the base would leave a bare sugar-phosphate, not a nucleoside; a nucleoside must still carry its base.
explanations.B: Incorrect. As with a purine base, removing the pyrimidine base would leave a sugar-phosphate rather than a nucleoside.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pentose sugar is a defining part of a nucleoside (base + sugar); removing it would leave a free base, not a nucleoside.
explanations.D: Correct. A nucleotide is a nucleoside (base + pentose sugar) with one or more phosphate groups attached. Hydrolysing that phosphate off leaves the base-sugar unit, which is exactly the definition of a nucleoside. This is the reverse of phosphorylating a nucleoside to build a nucleotide.

questions.title: Incorrect statement about cAMP
questions.question: As regards cAMP, one of the following is incorrect:

options.B: It is converted to 5' AMP by phosphomonoesterase

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP) as the first step of the classic G-protein/second-messenger cascade.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the false statement being asked for. cAMP is degraded to 5'-AMP by cAMP phosphodiesterase, an enzyme named for hydrolysing the phosphodiester bond within cAMP's cyclic structure. "Phosphomonoesterase" is not the correct enzyme name for this step, which is what makes this statement the incorrect one among the four.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). cAMP's principal downstream action is activating protein kinase A (PKA) by binding its regulatory subunits and releasing the catalytic subunits.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Epinephrine acting on Gs-coupled beta-adrenergic receptors stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP levels -- the classic hormone-triggered cAMP response.

questions.title: Ribose plus nitrogen base
questions.question: The chemical combination of ribose and one of the five nitrogen bases results in formation of a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A DNA molecule is a long polymer of many linked deoxyribonucleotides, not the product of combining one sugar with one base.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A nucleotide additionally requires a phosphate group; combining only ribose and a base gives a nucleoside, not a nucleotide.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A gene is a functional stretch of DNA sequence encoding a product, an entirely different level of organisation from a single sugar-base unit.
explanations.D: Correct. Joining a pentose sugar (here ribose) to one of the five nitrogenous bases via an N-glycosidic bond produces a nucleoside -- by definition, a base plus a sugar with no phosphate group involved. Adding one or more phosphate groups to this same nucleoside would then convert it into a nucleotide instead.

questions.title: Coenzyme A function
questions.question: Coenzyme A acts as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Methyl-donor duty belongs to SAM (S-adenosylmethionine), not Coenzyme A.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sulphate-donor duty belongs to PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine-5'-phosphosulphate), not Coenzyme A.
explanations.C: Correct. Coenzyme A's terminal thiol group forms a high-energy thioester bond with acyl groups (e.g. acetyl-CoA), making acyl-group transfer its defining biochemical role across fatty acid oxidation, the TCA cycle, and many other pathways.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hydrogen-carrier duty belongs to NAD+, FAD and NADP+; Coenzyme A, despite also being adenine-nucleotide derived, is explicitly not one of the hydrogen carriers.

questions.title: RNA type carrying genetic information to ribosomes
questions.question: Which of the following types of RNA carries the genetic information from DNA in the nucleus to the ribosomes for protein synthesis?

explanations.A: Correct. Messenger RNA (mRNA) is transcribed from nuclear DNA and carries that genetic code to the ribosome in the cytoplasm, where it is translated into protein -- its defining function among the RNA species. No other RNA type performs this specific carrier role.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is a structural and catalytic component of the ribosome itself; it does not carry genetic information from DNA to the ribosome.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Transfer RNA (tRNA) delivers amino acids to the ribosome during translation by matching its anticodon to the mRNA codon; it does not itself carry the DNA-derived genetic code.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Small RNAs (sRNA) have regulatory roles but are not the RNA species that carries the protein-coding genetic message from DNA to the ribosome.

questions.title: Protein not present within the core nucleosome
questions.question: One of the following proteins is not present within the core nucleosome:

explanations.A: Correct. The core nucleosome octamer is built from two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. Histone H1 is a separate "linker histone" that sits outside this core, binding linker DNA between adjacent nucleosomes and stabilising higher-order chromatin folding -- it is not one of the four core histone types.
explanations.B: Incorrect. H2A is one of the four core histone types (two copies per octamer) that the nucleosome's DNA wraps around.
explanations.C: Incorrect. H2B is likewise one of the four core histone types making up the nucleosome octamer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. H3 is likewise one of the four core histone types making up the nucleosome octamer.

questions.title: Guanine content from thymine content
questions.question: If a DNA molecule contains 30% thymine, then what is its guanine content?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 10% would leave the base percentages inconsistent with Chargaff's rule given 30% thymine -- see the correct calculation.
explanations.B: Correct. By Chargaff's rule, %A = %T, so adenine is also 30%, making A+T = 60% and leaving G+C = 40% of the molecule. Since %G = %C, guanine is half of that 40%, i.e. 20%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 30% would only be correct if it equalled thymine's own percentage, but this question asks for guanine, whose percentage is fixed by cytosine (G=C), not by thymine.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 40% is the combined G+C percentage (100% - 60% A+T), not guanine's own percentage; guanine alone is half of that, 20%.

questions.title: Bonds linking base pairs
questions.question: The bonds that link the base pairs in the DNA double helix are

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ionic bonds are not what pair complementary bases across the DNA double helix.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins; they play no role in base pairing within DNA.
explanations.C: Correct. Complementary bases across the two DNA strands (A-T, G-C) are held together by hydrogen bonds -- two between A and T, three between G and C -- which give the double helix its specific, reversible base pairing. This reversibility is what allows the strands to separate for replication and transcription without breaking the backbone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hydrophobic interactions contribute to base-stacking between adjacent bases along a strand, but they are not the bonds directly linking a base pair across the two strands.

questions.subtopic: Nucleic acid backbone chemistry and base pairing
questions.learning_objective: State that hydrogen bonds link the base pairs of the DNA double helix.

questions.title: False statement about tRNA structure
questions.question: As regards tRNA, all of the following statements are correct EXCEPT:

options.C: Has 5 loops and an acceptor arm

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). tRNA makes up a substantial minority fraction of cellular RNA, commonly cited around 15%, consistent with this statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Mature tRNA is well known for carrying multiple post-transcriptionally modified, unusual bases, including dihydrouracil and pseudouridine.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the false statement. Mature tRNA's cloverleaf structure has an acceptor stem plus roughly three main loops (the D-loop, the anticodon loop, and the T-psi-C loop, sometimes with a small variable loop) -- not five loops in addition to a separate acceptor arm. Overcounting the loops is a common structural-detail trap in tRNA questions.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). tRNA's characteristic secondary structure, drawn out flat, does form a recognisable cloverleaf shape.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: Identify that tRNA's cloverleaf structure has about three main loops plus an acceptor stem, not five loops.

questions.title: Composition of the nucleic acid backbone
questions.question: The "backbone" of a nucleic acid molecule consists of an alternating sequence of:

explanations.A: Correct. The nucleic acid backbone is built from alternating pentose sugar and phosphate groups, linked by phosphodiester bonds; the bases project outward from this backbone rather than being part of it. This backbone is identical in structure regardless of which bases the molecule happens to carry.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Sugar and base" describes a nucleoside unit, not the repeating backbone chain, which is sugar-phosphate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The backbone does not include the bases; phosphate alternates with sugar, not with base.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Including the base as a backbone component is incorrect -- the base is attached to (and projects from) the sugar-phosphate backbone, not part of its repeating chain.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nucleic acid backbone is an alternating sequence of sugar and phosphate groups.

questions.title: Codon and anticodon location
questions.question: The codon is found on ___, and the anticodon is found on ___.

explanations.A: Correct. The codon, a three-base sequence specifying an amino acid, is carried on mRNA; the complementary anticodon that reads it during translation is carried on tRNA. Base pairing between codon and anticodon is what matches each mRNA triplet to its correct amino acid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the correct assignment -- the codon is on mRNA, not tRNA, and the anticodon is on tRNA, not mRNA.
explanations.C: Incorrect. rRNA is a ribosomal structural/catalytic component; it does not carry the codon, which is on mRNA.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anticodon is carried on tRNA, not rRNA; rRNA has no anticodon role in translation.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: State that the codon is found on mRNA and the anticodon is found on tRNA.

questions.title: Correct statement about the DNA double helix
questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning the double helix structure present in DNA molecules is correct?

options.A: The two strands of DNA coil around a common axis to form a left-handed helix
options.B: Base pairing is always A-G and C-T
options.C: The sequence of the two strands is complementary and the sequence of one strand determines the sequence of the second one
options.D: The 2 strands of DNA run parallel to each other

explanations.A: Incorrect. Standard B-DNA is a right-handed helix, not left-handed; Z-DNA is the left-handed form, but it is not the default double helix this statement describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Standard Watson-Crick base pairing is A-T and G-C, not A-G and C-T -- A-G and C-T are not valid complementary pairs.
explanations.C: Correct. The two DNA strands are fully complementary: because of strict A-T/G-C pairing, the base sequence of one strand entirely determines the sequence of the other, which is the basis of DNA replication and repair. Each parental strand can therefore template a new complementary strand with no ambiguity.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The two strands of DNA run antiparallel (one 5'->3', the other 3'->5'), not parallel to each other.

questions.subtopic: Nucleic acid backbone chemistry and base pairing
questions.learning_objective: Identify the correct statement about DNA double helix structure: strand complementarity.

questions.title: Bonds holding the DNA backbone together
questions.question: The nucleotides in the backbone of DNA are held together by ___ bonds.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together across the helix (base pairing), not successive nucleotides within one strand's backbone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peptide bonds link amino acids in proteins, not nucleotides in a nucleic acid backbone.
explanations.C: Correct. Successive nucleotides within a DNA strand are joined by phosphodiester bonds, linking the 3' carbon of one sugar to the 5' phosphate of the next, forming the repeating backbone chain. This linkage is what gives each strand its 5' to 3' directionality.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A glycosidic bond joins a base to its own sugar within one nucleotide; it does not link adjacent nucleotides to each other.

questions.learning_objective: State that phosphodiester bonds hold successive nucleotides together in the DNA backbone.

questions.title: Guanine and cytosine equality in DNA
questions.question: In DNA molecule

options.A: The number of guanine bases does not equal cytosine bases
options.B: The number of adenine bases does not equal thymine bases
options.C: The number of adenine bases equals uracil bases
options.D: The number of guanine bases equals cytosine bases

explanations.A: Incorrect. Because every guanine pairs with a cytosine across the double helix, guanine and cytosine counts are always equal in double-stranded DNA -- the opposite of this statement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because every adenine pairs with a thymine, adenine and thymine counts are always equal in double-stranded DNA -- the opposite of this statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. DNA does not contain uracil at all (RNA does); this comparison is not meaningful for DNA.
explanations.D: Correct. Because every guanine on one strand pairs with a cytosine on the complementary strand, a DNA molecule's total guanine count always equals its total cytosine count -- one part of Chargaff's rule (the other being A=T). This equality holds regardless of the actual GC content of the specific DNA molecule.

questions.learning_objective: State that guanine and cytosine base counts are equal in double-stranded DNA (Chargaff's rule).

questions.title: False characteristic of transfer RNA
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of transfer RNA?

options.C: A given transfer RNA can carry any of the 20 amino acids

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true of tRNA). tRNA's secondary structure does form a recognisable cloverleaf shape.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true of tRNA). Mature tRNA is well known for its many post-transcriptionally modified, unusual bases.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the false statement. Each tRNA species is charged, by its own specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, with only the one amino acid matching its anticodon; it is not a generic carrier able to deliver any of the 20 standard amino acids. This specificity is essential to the fidelity of the genetic code's translation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true of tRNA). Every tRNA carries an anticodon loop that base-pairs with the mRNA codon during translation.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: State that a given tRNA molecule carries only its one specific amino acid, not any of the 20.

questions.title: Why RNA base counts need not follow Chargaff's rule
questions.question: In RNA molecule guanine bases does not necessarily equal its cytosine bases also, its adenine bases does not necessarily equal its uracil bases since it is a

explanations.A: Correct. Chargaff's rule (%A=%T or %U, %G=%C) arises from obligate complementary base pairing across two strands. Because RNA is typically single stranded, it has no obligate partner strand enforcing that equality, so its base percentages need not satisfy the rule.
explanations.B: Incorrect. RNA being "double stranded" is not the reason its base counts are unequal -- in fact a double-stranded molecule is exactly what would enforce Chargaff-style base equality, the opposite of what is observed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. As with "double stranded molecule", a double-stranded helical structure would enforce, not break, base-count equality; this does not explain RNA's unequal base counts.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Being a "polymer of purine ribonucleotides" is not an accurate description of RNA (which contains both purine and pyrimidine ribonucleotides) and is not the reason for its unequal base counts.

questions.subtopic: Nucleic acid backbone chemistry and base pairing
questions.learning_objective: Explain that RNA's base counts do not obey Chargaff's rule because RNA is single stranded.

questions.title: Composition of histones
questions.question: As regards histones of chromatid:

options.C: They are basic proteins rich in lysine and arginine

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histones are basic, not acidic, proteins -- their basicity is what lets them bind DNA's negatively charged phosphate backbone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Histones are positively charged (basic), not negatively charged; their positive charge is what attracts them electrostatically to DNA's negatively charged backbone.
explanations.C: Correct. Histones are basic proteins, rich in the basic amino acids lysine and arginine, which gives them the positive charge needed to bind DNA's negatively charged phosphate backbone electrostatically. This binding compacts DNA into nucleosomes and higher-order chromatin structure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There are five main histone types (H1, H2A, H2B, H3 and H4), not four.

questions.learning_objective: State that histones are basic proteins rich in lysine and arginine.

questions.title: Incorrect statement about mitochondrial DNA
questions.question: One of the following concerning mitochondrial DNA is incorrect:

options.A: Mitochondrial DNA is present in the form of a small single stranded circular supercoil
options.C: Mutations of mitochondrial DNA are associated with certain types of myopathies
options.D: Mitochondrial DNA forms 0.3 to 1% of the total cellular DNA

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the false statement. Mitochondrial DNA is a small, double-stranded circular molecule, not single stranded; calling it single stranded is the error among these four statements. Its double-stranded circular form resembles a bacterial chromosome more than the linear nuclear chromosomes.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Mitochondrial DNA is inherited maternally, since mitochondria (and their DNA) are passed down almost exclusively through the ovum.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Mitochondrial DNA mutations are well recognised causes of mitochondrial myopathies and related multisystem disorders.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is true). Mitochondrial DNA is commonly cited as forming roughly 0.3-1% of total cellular DNA, reflecting the many mitochondria (each with multiple DNA copies) per cell relative to the single nuclear genome.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that mitochondrial DNA is double-stranded and circular, not single stranded.

questions.title: Definition of DNA melting temperature
questions.question: The melting temperature of DNA is the temperature at which:

options.C: DNA changes from double helix into supercoiled DNA
options.D: Half of the helical structure of DNA is lost

explanations.A: Incorrect. DNA melting is not a solid-to-liquid phase change; it refers to strand denaturation within solution, not a physical state change of a solid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Melting is a physical unwinding of the double helix (denaturation), not a chemical hydrolysis that breaks the molecule down into its individual nucleotides.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Melting denatures the double helix into single strands; it does not convert the helix into a "supercoiled" form.
explanations.D: Correct. The melting temperature (Tm) is defined as the temperature at which half of the double-helical base pairing has denatured into single strands, commonly tracked by the rise in UV absorbance as stacked, paired bases separate. This denaturation is reversible on cooling, which is why hybridisation techniques rely on it.

questions.learning_objective: Define the melting temperature of DNA as the point at which half of its helical structure is denatured.

questions.title: Composition of a nucleoside
questions.question: A nucleoside consists of

explanations.A: Incorrect. A nitrogenous base alone (with no sugar attached) is not a nucleoside; the sugar is a required component.
explanations.B: Correct. A nucleoside is a purine or pyrimidine base joined to a pentose sugar, with no phosphate group involved. Adding phosphate to this same unit converts it into a nucleotide instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Base + phosphorous" omits the sugar and wrongly includes phosphate, describing neither a nucleoside nor a standard nucleotide correctly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option both wrongly requires both a purine and a pyrimidine base together (a nucleoside has one base, not both types) and wrongly includes phosphate, which would make it a nucleotide definition at best, not a nucleoside.

questions.learning_objective: Define a nucleoside as a purine or pyrimidine base joined to a sugar.

questions.title: Identifying a purine nucleotide
questions.question: A purine nucleotide is:

explanations.A: Correct. AMP (adenosine monophosphate) contains adenine, a purine base, making it a purine nucleotide. Guanine is the only other purine base, so AMP and GMP are the two purine nucleotides among the standard ribonucleotides.
explanations.B: Incorrect. UMP contains uracil, a pyrimidine base, making it a pyrimidine nucleotide, not a purine one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CMP contains cytosine, a pyrimidine base, making it a pyrimidine nucleotide, not a purine one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. TMP contains thymine, a pyrimidine base, making it a pyrimidine nucleotide, not a purine one.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: Identify AMP as a purine nucleotide, distinguishing it from the pyrimidine nucleotides UMP, CMP and TMP.

questions.title: Pyrimidine high-energy intermediate
questions.question: The pyrimidine nucleotide acting as the high energy intermediate is

explanations.A: Incorrect. ATP is a purine nucleotide (it contains adenine), not a pyrimidine one, so it does not fit what this question asks for despite also being a high-energy compound.
explanations.B: Correct. UTP is the pyrimidine nucleotide that functions as a high-energy intermediate, most notably reacting with glucose-1-phosphate to form UDP-glucose, the activated sugar donor for glycogen synthesis and other glycosylation reactions. This mirrors ATP's high-energy role among the purine nucleotides.
explanations.C: Incorrect. UDP-Glc (UDP-glucose) is itself a downstream product formed using UTP's energy, not the high-energy intermediate being asked for.
explanations.D: Incorrect. CMP is a low-energy pyrimidine monophosphate, not a high-energy intermediate.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: Identify UTP as the pyrimidine nucleotide serving as a high-energy intermediate.

questions.title: Location of the tRNA CCA sequence
questions.question: Although each specific tRNA differs from the others in its sequence of nucleotides, all tRNA molecules contain a base paired stem that terminates in the sequence CCA at:

explanations.A: Correct. Every mature tRNA carries a conserved, unpaired CCA sequence at its 3' terminus; the free 3'-OH of the terminal adenosine is where the amino acid is esterified during aminoacylation. This conserved end is the same across all tRNA species despite their differing internal sequences.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The conserved CCA sequence is at the 3' terminus, not the 5' terminus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The anticodon arm is a different structural region (where the anticodon loop base-pairs with the mRNA codon); the conserved CCA sequence is at the 3' terminus, not on the anticodon arm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The CCA sequence is specifically at the 3' terminus, not split across or spanning both termini.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: State that all tRNA molecules carry the conserved CCA sequence at their 3' terminus.

questions.title: Base defining the tRNA D-arm
questions.question: In tRNA molecule D arm is named for the presence of the base:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Uracil is a standard RNA base found throughout tRNA, but it is not the specific unusual base that names the D-arm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pseudouridine ("pseudouracil") is the unusual base concentrated in the T-psi-C arm, not the D-arm.
explanations.C: Correct. The D-arm of tRNA is named for its concentration of dihydrouracil, an unusual base formed by post-transcriptional reduction of a uracil ring double bond. This is the same base-arm relationship tested from the reverse direction elsewhere in this bank.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thymine is not typically found in tRNA in the way described here, and it is the T-psi-C arm (via pseudouridine), not the D-arm, that carries a thymine-related base.

questions.subtopic: Nucleotide/coenzyme identification and tRNA structure
questions.learning_objective: State that the tRNA D-arm is named for the unusual base dihydrouracil.

questions.title: Adenine content from guanosine content
questions.question: In a DNA molecule, if the guanosine content is 40%, the adenine content will be:

explanations.A: Correct. By Chargaff's rule, %G = %C, so cytosine is also 40%, making G+C = 80% and leaving A+T = 20% of the molecule. Since %A = %T, adenine is half of that 20%, i.e. 10%.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 20% is the combined A+T percentage (100% - 80% G+C), not adenine's own percentage; adenine alone is half of that, 10%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 30% is not consistent with the calculation given 40% guanosine content.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 40% would only be correct if adenine equalled guanine's own percentage, but adenine's percentage is fixed by thymine (A=T), not by guanine.

questions.title: Basis of DNA double helix stability
questions.question: The structural stability of the double helix of DNA is mainly due to:

options.A: Hydrogen bonding between adjacent purine bases
options.B: Hydrophobic bonding between stacked purine and pyrimidine nuclei
options.C: Hydrogen bonding between adjacent pyrimidine bases
options.D: Hydrogen bonding between purine and pyrimidine bases

explanations.A: Incorrect. Normal Watson-Crick pairing does not hydrogen-bond two purines together; a purine on one strand pairs with a pyrimidine on the other.
explanations.B: Incorrect per this source's key. Base-stacking (hydrophobic/van der Waals interactions between adjacent stacked bases) does contribute to overall duplex stability in general biochemistry, but this source specifically keys the double helix's structural stability to purine-pyrimidine hydrogen bonding rather than stacking.
explanations.C: Incorrect. As with two purines, normal Watson-Crick pairing does not hydrogen-bond two pyrimidines together.
explanations.D: Correct, per this source. The DNA double helix's base pairing -- and the stability this source attributes to it -- comes from hydrogen bonding specifically between complementary purine and pyrimidine bases (A-T, G-C) across the two strands, not between two bases of the same class. Base-stacking also contributes to overall duplex stability in fuller treatments, but this is the mechanism this source's key points to.
